title: Council Post: The Role Of AI In Reshaping The Industrial World
text:
Ujjwal Kumar is Group President at Teradyne Robotics.
The history of robots in manufacturing goes back to 1962, when a 4,000-pound, one-armed robot named Unimate was installed at a GM plant in Trenton, New Jersey to lift and stack hot pieces of metal. It was a revolution in manufacturing, but only the first of many. Today, the integration of AI in manufacturing promises to transform the industrial sector just as much as Unimate did, provided organizations can overcome adoption challenges and embrace cultural and structural changes.
The combination of AI and advanced robotics can be an amazing symbiotic relationship, although we are still in the early stages of developing use cases. Companies are developing “cobots” (collaborative robots) equipped with AI that can learn and adapt to new tasks. Deep learning algorithms can analyze high-resolution images to detect and remove obstacles in real time. The overall goal is to add AI algorithms to the new generation of advanced robotics to further unlock quick deployment and seamless operations in high variability and even unstructured real-life applications.
Adoption Challenges
Traditional industrial robots excel at repetitive tasks on high-volume production lines. However, manufacturing environments increasingly involve low-volume production with frequent variations. Robots programmed for specific tasks may not be able to handle unexpected variations in product type or placement. While AI can offer some flexibility, figuring out how to make AI-powered robots flexible enough to handle unpredictable environments will be crucial.
Manufacturers that plan to incorporate AI need workers who understand both the physical processes of their industry and the complexities of AI. On one hand, you need to have a human in the loop who knows how to get the most value out of an AI algorithm. This is where skills like interpreting data visualizations, AI-generated reports and troubleshooting unexpected results are important. On the other hand, you need to have someone to program and often reprogram the robot, to ensure that it’s functioning at maximum efficiency. It can be hard to find workers with these combined skill sets.
AI technologies, especially generative models, can function like a black box. The reasoning behind their answers isn’t clear, and why they give different results at different times can be a mystery. This lack of transparency can make manufacturers hesitant to rely on AI for crucial decisions in their operations. If you don't understand why an AI recommends a certain action, it can be difficult to trust its decisions, especially for critical tasks. Without understanding the logic behind the answer, troubleshooting becomes more complex.
Impact On The Workforce
A common narrative about AI—as it was in the past about robots—is that these tools are going to automate away large segments of the workforce. At the firm level, we see quite the opposite. As companies invest in these new technologies, they end up hiring more people in more fulfilling roles, leading to increased productivity, competitiveness and worker satisfaction.
However, there are still challenges in upskilling the workforce to adapt to these technologies. Best practices involve introducing more robots while upskilling your workers to handle more complex tasks. Instead of having one worker operate one machine, for example, they can now operate a group of machines.
Leadership And Cultural Transformation
The successful integration of AI and robotics first requires that business leaders at the highest levels understand the huge potential benefit this transformation will have. This will require change from top to bottom, including restructuring processes and workflows and empowering “technology champions” on the factory floor and empowering them to lead others. Domain expertise will also be crucial to interpret and validate the vast amount of new information AI generates.
Even though the industrial sector tends to be conservative, it can transform rapidly once the operational benefits of new technologies become clear. Think about introducing personal computers to the office in the 1970s and ‘80s: The most successful companies were the ones that transformed their organizational structure to integrate the new machines instead of trying to layer them on top of existing organizational structures. As the industrial sector continues to evolve, companies that can thoughtfully integrate AI with robotics while prioritizing workforce development and organizational restructuring will have the highest odds of long-term success.

title: Council Post: In Today’s 'Trust Nothing' Era, Identity Verification Reigns Supreme
text:
Chief Product Officer - Ping Identity.
With the rise of digital technologies creating a more interconnected world, organizations face an increasing number of threats—with fraud being one of the most pervasive and damaging to a business and customers. Fraudulent activities, ranging from identity theft to financial scams, can wreak havoc on a business, leading to financial losses, reputational damage and regulatory scrutiny.
Making matters worse, artificial intelligence (AI) has infiltrated organizations rapidly. If 2023 was the year where AI emerged onto the scene, then 2024 is the year of AI implementation within businesses—streamlining tedious, traditionally manual tasks and processes. But AI also brings risks, providing opportunistic cybercriminals with additional resources to lure victims and fuel fraudulent attacks. Forty-one percent of senior decision-makers expect cybercriminals’ use of AI to significantly increase identity threats over the next year, and nearly half (48%) are not very confident they have the right technology in place to defend against these AI attacks.
As the risk of fraud continues to evolve and AI drastically changes the threat landscape, we need a new way to think about—and respond to—the challenges around security and identity fraud. Businesses must prioritize identity verification and ensure people are who they claim they are. After all, we have entered the era of “trust nothing, verify everything”—and most organizations are not prepared for it.
Step 1: Understanding The Widespread Risks And Latest Tactics
The first step in combating fraud is understanding its prevalence and impact on organizations. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) reported consumers lost more than $10 billion to fraud in 2023, a 14% increase over reported losses in 2022. Fraud is not limited to any particular industry or region. It can affect organizations of all sizes and across all sectors, from financial services to healthcare to retail.
It’s also important to understand the latest techniques fraudsters are using to launch successful attacks. For example, the advancements in generative AI have made deepfakes a regular occurrence. Deepfakes, or an artificial image or video generated by AI/ML capabilities, don’t just impersonate celebrities—they are now cloning company leaders, from the CEO to CFO and beyond. These types of realistic, targeted impersonations make it very easy for an employee to click on a fraudulent link or provide the sensitive information the deepfakes may be asking for. Traditional security training curricula don’t account for deepfakes; as an industry, we need to raise greater awareness of this new technique before businesses face the drastic consequences.
Step 2: Prioritizing Identity Verification
One of the key strategies for combating AI-based fraud is identity verification. By strongly verifying the identity of individuals accessing their systems, organizations can significantly reduce the risk of fraudulent activities. For example, financial institutions use identity verification to prevent unauthorized access to customer accounts and protect against identity theft. Identity verification involves verifying that an individual is who they claim to be, typically through a combination of factors such as passwords, biometric data, document verification and knowledge-based questions.
In the age of AI, when trust is no longer implicit, identity verification is more critical than ever. AI-powered tools can help organizations detect and prevent fraud in real time by analyzing vast amounts of data to identify suspicious patterns and behaviors. For example, AI can analyze a customer's purchasing history and behavior to detect any anomalies that may indicate fraudulent activity. These tools can help organizations identify potential fraudsters before they can cause any damage, saving businesses time and money in the process.
However, despite the recognized importance of advanced protection technologies like multifactor authentication (MFA) and biometrics, only 45% of organizations use two-factor/multifactor identification verification to protect against fraud, and even less (44%) use biometrics.
Step 3: Futureproofing Protection With Decentralized Identity
Identity verification is critical to protect against fraud today, but to take protection one step further, decentralized identity (DCI) is emerging as a smart solution to combat fraud—now just now, but for the future, as well. Decentralized identity is an emerging concept intended to give control back to consumers through the use of an identity wallet. We’re seeing DCI case studies take off over the past few years. For example, many states within the U.S. are implementing digital wallets within departments of motor vehicles, as we witnessed in California.
Nearly 60% of businesses believe that DCI will be “highly valuable” to their organization, not only enhancing security but also providing opportunities for better customer experiences and reduced business overhead. But of course, like with any new technologies, organizations may be hesitant to implement it—but it is the future, and the early innovators and adopters will rise above the noise and better protect against fraud long term.
Fraud is a pervasive and evolving threat that organizations must address proactively. By understanding the risks and implementing effective strategies such as AI-powered fraud detection and identity verification, organizations can significantly reduce their risk exposure and protect themselves against financial and reputational damage. In the age of AI, staying ahead of threat actors requires constant vigilance and a commitment to implementing the latest technologies and best practices in fraud prevention. Are you prepared?

title: Council Post: The Algorithmic Magnetic Effect: Can Employer Branding Hack AI To Attract The Right Talent?
text:
Founder and CEO of Valuematrix.ai. A Nasscom Deeptech and CII Mentor who's associated with many startups in the AI and SaaS space.
Companies are battling an unprecedented tech talent shortage in the hyper-competitive job market. The brightest minds in technology have their pick of lucrative job offers. Employers must find ways to rise above the noise and capture candidates' attention to hire and retain the skills they need.
One powerful strategy is to leverage AI technology and smart employer branding tactics. By optimizing digital employer branding content for machine learning models, companies can essentially "hack" algorithms to put their opportunity in front of ideal candidates at key moments.
How AI Is Reshaping The Talent Acquisition Landscape
The rise of AI recruitment tools powered by natural language processing (NLP) has significantly disrupted and optimized talent acquisition. Intelligent matching algorithms can now automatically surface and prioritize top applicants from resume databases. The current hiring process supports chatbots in conducting initial screenings and scheduling interviews. AI can even analyze a candidate's social media presence and online footprint to assess cultural fit.
AI-powered recruitment tools are a massive timesaver for tech talent navigating a saturated job market. Top candidates don't have to sift through hundreds of mediocre opportunities—AI models bring them hyper-personalized role matches based on their skills, experiences and cultural alignment. AI can help predict if the candidate is the right addition to an organization’s team dynamics. For instance, it can help predict if the candidate can work smoothly with their manager or other team members and ensure a higher success rate in their new roles.
AI's pivotal role in hiring makes deploying an AI-focused employer branding strategy mission-critical for companies wanting to attract elite tech talent.
Hacking The Algorithm With Strategic Employer Branding
Investing in a compelling, authentic employer brand is the first step to gaining an algorithmic advantage. Companies need to define and broadcast their unique value proposition for tech talent: What makes working at their organization rewarding and fulfilling? What differentiates their approach, culture, benefits and growth opportunities?
With their employer branding positioning clarified, companies can optimize their recruitment marketing content accordingly. AI language models are trained to identify context and meaning from written content, such as:
• Job descriptions.
• Company career site pages.
• Recruitment marketing materials.
• Social media content promoting open roles.
Implementing role-specific keywords and skills nomenclature into employer branding assets can significantly boost a company's search result rankings and visibility within AI recruitment platforms. Tech talent looking for specific job titles, responsibilities or required skills will be automatically served that company's opportunity.
Additionally, many job search sites and tools rely on extracting rich metadata about companies from online content. Consistent publishing of branded content spotlighting the organization's inner workings, tech stack, product roadmaps and employee spotlights educates AI models to recognize the business as an attractive landing spot for candidates matched to those attributes.
In essence, companies can increase their "magnetic" effect for AI recruitment technology by purposefully optimizing their digital employer brand presence to match the attributes of their ideal candidates. Staying top of mind with skilled technologists doesn't require mega-budgets or splashy marketing campaigns in this AI-driven landscape—it simply requires speaking the same "language" as the algorithms matching talent to opportunity.
The War For Tech Talent Demands Innovative Strategies

title: Qualcomm Stock Is Up 40% This Year As AI And Auto Business Surge
text:
Mobile chipset major Qualcomm (NASDAQ: QCOM) has seen its stock rise by a solid 41% year-to-date. There have been several factors driving the recent gains for the company, including signs of a recovery in the smartphone market and optimism that the generative AI trend will help smartphone sales. Qualcomm also published a better-than-expected set of Q2 FY’24 results last month, with guidance for Q3 also coming ahead of estimates. The company sees revenue of between $8.8 billion and $9.6 billion for Q3, marking an increase of over 13% at the upper end of guidance, with earnings coming in at between $2.15 and $2.35 per share.
While the smartphone market saw a lull in 2023, as the Covid-19 pandemic eased and economic uncertainty weighed on consumer spending, things have been looking up of late. Per Canalys, worldwide smartphone shipments grew 11% year on year over the first quarter of 2024. This is helping Qualcomm’s CDMA Technologies segment, which supplies application processors, modems, and software for mobile devices, networking equipment, and consumer electronics.
The surging interest in generative artificial intelligence is also benefiting Qualcomm. The company is seeing higher demand for high-end chipsets such as the Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 that are optimized for AI, including enhancing voice assistants and generating images. Moreover, Qualcomm is also seeing higher demand from China, where local OEMs have increased their uptake by over 40% compared to last year, as demand for premium Android devices grows at the expense of Apple’s iPhone. Qualcomm’s chips also appear to be gaining traction in the PC market, as vendors look to deploy AI natively into computers. In May, Microsoft and other Windows PC players announced new computers with artificial intelligence features using chips including Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X Elite and Snapdragon X Plus processors. The X Elite processor has an integrated NPU (Neural Processing Unit) which is specifically designed for executing machine learning algorithms.
Qualcomm’s automotive business is also faring well as semiconductors play a much bigger role in the transportation industry with trends such as electrification and autonomous driving gathering pace. Semiconductor content in vehicles has also been soaring. Per Deloitte, electronics account for 40% of a new vehicle’s total cost, up from under 20% in 2000. The number is likely to grow to over 45% by the end of this decade. Qualcomm’s automotive revenues rose by 35% year-over-year in Q2 FY’24 to $603 million. The company’s Snapdragon Digital Chassis solution - which is a set of cloud-connected platforms for telematics and connectivity in cars - now has a design win pipeline of roughly $45 billion. Qualcomm indicates that it is gaining market share, remaining on track for over $4 billion in automotive revenue by FY’26.
Now the optimism surrounding artificial intelligence and Qualcomm’s automotive business has driven its stock up 35% from levels of $150 in early January 2021 to around $205 now, vs. an increase of about 40% for the S&P 500 over this roughly 3-year period. That said, the increase in QCOM stock has been far from consistent. Returns for the stock were 20% in 2021, -40% in 2022, and 32% in 2023. In comparison, returns for the S&P 500 have been 27% in 2021, -19% in 2022, and 24% in 2023 - indicating that QCOM underperformed the broader indices in 2021 and 2022.
In contrast, the Trefis High Quality Portfolio has outperformed the S&P 500 each year over the same period, providing better returns while taking on less risk versus the benchmark index. Less of a roller coaster ride, as is evident in HQ Portfolio performance metrics. Given the uncertain macroeconomic environment with elevated interest rates, could QCOM face a similar situation as it did in 2021 and 2022 and underperform the S&P over the next 12 months - or will it see a strong jump?
Qualcomm stock trades at just about $204 per share, or about 22x consensus FY’24 earnings. Although this isn’t exactly a high multiple, there are some concerns. Qualcomm’s revenues are likely to see little growth this year. Moreover, competition in the company’s core mobile chipset space is also mounting. For instance, China’s Huawei’s new smartphones will feature its proprietary Kirin processors going forward, leading to lower sales for Qualcomm. There is also speculation that Samsung could also drop Qualcomm processors on its upcoming flagship in favor of its own Exynos line of chips. We have a $189 price estimate for Qualcomm, which is slightly below the current market price of $204.
