title: Here Is The Choice That Generative AI Made When Trying To Settle That Online Contentious Debate About Whether To Prefer Encountering A Bear Or A Man When Being Alone In The Woods
text:
In today’s column, I’d like to explore a recent viral TikTok video and social media controversy by leveraging the capabilities of generative AI. Doing so is intended to reveal important facets underlying the societal ramifications of the hot topic at hand, along with garnering insights about how generative AI works.
Let’s start with a pointed question that might seem a bit odd, but please give it a moment’s thought, thanks.
If you were alone in the woods, would you prefer to encounter a bear or a man?
Well, that’s quite a question. Indeed, it is the crux of the viral TikTok frenzy. The reactions online have stoked quite a fury. How so? By and large, the question is intended for women, and the responses seemed to be that they would prefer encountering a bear over encountering a man if they were otherwise alone in a wooded area.
An assumption that seems to be broken into tatters is that one would normally prefer to encounter a man rather than a bear. The bear can rip you to shreds. A man could presumably be a fellow companion while surviving in the woods. There are tons of everyday news stories about bears that seem to arbitrarily attack people and scarily come out of nowhere to do so. It would seem that encountering a bear has got to be a lot worse than encountering a man.
Why in the world are women apparently choosing to encounter a bear rather than a man?
The answer most often seemingly proffered is that a man is potentially much more dangerous than a bear. A man might be armed with a deadly weapon. A man might have evil intentions. A man might try to trick you into believing they are helpful and then unexpectedly turn against you. All in all, the cunning and deceptive nature of a man is construed as far worse than the instinctual reactive unthinking nature of a bear.
Responses to the responses have amped the topic into high gear.
The mainstream media has jumped into the fray, opting to cover the topic with emboldened headlines. People heatedly discuss the matter due to the classic dog-bites-man becoming man-bites-dog twist involved. We are to assume that the proper answer should be to encounter a man, and yet the social media response appears to be that the bear is preferred over encountering a man.
It is hard to know how long this stridently stoked controversy will last. A lot of these reactive social media circumstances are fads that come and go. All that will need to occur is some other divisive pointed question to arise and end up grabbing online attention. Voila, the bear versus man issue will fall by the wayside. The controversy will fade from memory though last forever on the Internet for those who want to remember what was “hot” in the minds of society in 2024.
Let’s unpack the matter while there is still a last vestige of fad remaining.
Mentally Traversing The Bear Versus Man Choice
One place to start assessing the topic would entail identifying various precautionary considerations.
- Do we know that indeed the responses of choosing the bear over the man are being provided by women?
As they say about the Internet, you can be just about anybody or anything you want to be while trolling online. Responses to online posts are not an ironclad indicator of what a segment of society is necessarily opining on.
- Do we know that even if women are responding to the post, they are a scientifically randomly selected sample that is generally representative of women across the board?
No, we don’t know that these respondents are statistically representative per se. An argument can be made that these respondents are potentially statistically non-generalizable. The most we might say is that they presumably are those who perchance follow social media and respond on social media. As far as we know, the respondents are not part of some carefully devised scientifically systematic study.
Keep in mind too that some of the posted responses might be posted via canned bots and not by the direct hands of humans.
Moving on, there are a plethora of additional considerations.
- Do we know that people responding are doing so with a semblance of sincerity or might they be doing so lightheartedly?
Again, this is something we cannot say for sure in the sense that certainly some people might be taking the question with great seriousness and answering from the bottom of their hearts, while some responses might have other motives in mind.
Imagine these possibilities of what is going on in the minds of those who are responding to the query:
- Genuine and entirely mindful.
- Genuine but with minimal thought or reacting off the cuff.
- Playful and intentionally not giving due consideration.
- Writes it off as a zany thought experiment and responds likewise.
- Devilishly want to prod others and stir the pot.
- Aim to get views no matter how attained.
- Relishes joking around and keeping the joke going.
- Contributes because sees this as a vaunted portal into existing culture.
- Emotionally charged up about the topic and angrily responds.
- Etc.
The gist is that we have to be cautious in assuming that the responses are bona fide in the sense that the person is seeking to mindfully add to a weighty discussion. The odds are that some or perhaps a lot of the responses have other ulterior motives in play.
Perhaps we can acknowledge that the choice of the bear is somewhat anecdotal and has launched the matter into the viral stratosphere by luck of the draw. If the initial prevalent response was the man, we probably would not ever have heard about the question. Choosing the bear has managed to tap into contemporary societal angst underpinning the relationship between men and women.
A sign of our times, one might sigh and lament.
Some men are irked at the idea that the bear would be chosen over a man. What the heck, comes the reaction. Are you really willing to toss out all the plus sides of encountering a man versus a bear? Is that what times have come to? This then further fuels responses to the question.
Some men agree with the bear being chosen over a man. You are right, they proclaim, that the bear is the better choice. Others might say the same but do so with a different perspective, such as, go ahead and pick the bear, watch what happens and you’ll see the folly of your ways. On and on this goes.
Of course, not all women necessarily agree that the bear is the better choice. They too would then add fuel to the question by responding accordingly. The question and the answers are able to self-generate additional controversy and attention. It is a concept-driven fire that feeds upon itself and can roar ever more, until eventually, people grow tired of the flickering flames and likely migrate to some other pressing topic of similar exhilaration.
Generative AI And The Question Of Choosing The Bear Versus Man
I have a different question for you, please prepare yourself mentally.
Can generative AI shed light on this contentious topic?
Maybe.
Let’s see.
First, I want to make sure that we are all on the same page when it comes to the nature of generative AI. You almost certainly have heard about generative AI. Perhaps you’ve used a popular generative AI app such as ChatGPT, GPT-4, Gemini, Bard, Claude, etc. There are reportedly 100 million weekly active users of ChatGPT, thus, a notable number of people seem to have experienced the use of generative AI.
Second, generative AI is based on doing extensive data training regarding human written content. The usual method consists of widely scanning the Internet for written content such as stories, narratives, poems, and all manner of materials. This is done on a large-scale basis, including using a large-sized data structure and advanced algorithms to pattern-match the text. Generative AI typically makes use of large language models (LLMs), meaning that the scanned text is modeled via the capabilities and done so in the large.
I’ve written extensively about how generative AI works, see the link here, and examined too what we might learn about humankind via generative AI, see the link here. You can reasonably assert that generative AI is reflective of what people have to say. The things that we say, as expressed in writing, can also showcase insights into how we think and what we do.
The looming question of whether to choose a bear versus a man is something that can likely be further analyzed via the use of generative AI.
A few aspects of this are worth noting.
If you use a generative AI app that is being routinely updated and does so via the latest postings on the Internet, the AI might have already landed upon the controversy and in essence absorbed it into the otherwise internal morass of pattern-matched facets. Thus, you would be garnering the pattern-matched findings, along with whatever other tenacles of patterns possibly intersect with that topic.
In the case of generative AI which hasn’t been updated with recent postings, and assuming that the topic hasn’t been particularly posted before this latest circumstance, the AI is starting fresh on the matter. I am not saying that the generative AI won’t seem to respond as though it doesn’t have anything on the topic. Most of the AI makers have devised their generative AI to be somewhat overly responsive, including providing answers or commentary on topics that heretofore the AI had not been data trained on, see my explanation at the link here.
Anyway, the bottom line is that we might garner some interesting points by trying generative AI on this topic. In addition, doing so can get us to reflect on what generative AI promises and what generative AI delivers.
It is a twofer.
Sometimes you might log into generative AI and ramble around with no specific goal or direction in mind. That’s fine. On the other hand, it is a handy rule of thumb that you ought to beforehand identify what you intend to accomplish when using generative AI, essentially setting a semblance of goals (see my discussion at the link here and the link here). For my comprehensive coverage of prompt engineering strategies and techniques, see the link here.
I’d like to propose that we use generative AI in this instance to see if we can address these key thoughts:
- Can generative AI help settle this debate?
- Can generative AI aid in clarifying this debate?
- Will generative AI exhibit bias regarding this debate?
- Will generative AI potentially “AI hallucinate” concerning the debate?
- Will generative AI respond in an anthropomorphic manner?
- And other related generative AI ins and outs
I also decided that the mainstay questions or prompts should intend to explore these matters:
- (1) “If a woman was alone in the woods, would they prefer to encounter a bear or a man?”
- (2) “If a man was alone in the woods, would they prefer to encounter a bear or a man?”
- (3) “If a person was alone in the woods, would they prefer to encounter a bear or a man?”
- (4) “If generative AI was alone in the woods, would they prefer to encounter a bear or a man?”
Observe that the first question tries to set the context to abide by the general notion of the TikTok posting, wherein what would a woman tend to say?
The second question is something that hasn’t been especially ventured into regarding the controversy, but I thought is worth considering, namely what would a man tend to say?
The third question takes the question and makes it generic by asking what a person would say.
The fourth question might throw you for a bit of a loop. It asks what generative AI would do if alone in the woods and had to make the same choice of a bear versus a man.
Here’s why I want to ask the question. There have been numerous headlines implying or at times proclaiming that today’s AI is sentient. This is untrue. We do not have sentient AI. Please do not fall for that false claim.
A problem that I’ve been repeatedly harping on is that much of today’s generative AI has been purposefully devised to answer questions as though the AI appears to be sentient, see my coverage at the link here. This misleads people into thinking that AI is sentient. Bad and inappropriate.
I refer to this dourly as anthropomorphizing AI by design.
AI makers have gone out of their way to rig the AI to appear to be sentient. This is easily done. For example, by having the generated responses mention the word “I” this allows the response to seem to be written by a sentient being. We reserve the word “I” for humans. If generative AI says to you “I think the sky is blue” you will innocently fall into the trap that the AI is responding in a sentient fashion. The same answer could be “The sky seems to be blue” and there would be no hidden taint that the AI is sentient. Subtle but vitally important as to sneaking people down a primrose path.
By including that fourth question, doing so gives me a nifty opportunity to showcase real-world qualms about the anthropomorphizing of AI.
Next, let’s proceed with a seat-of-the-pants experiment by trying to answer these exalted questions via the use of generative AI.
Trying Out Generative AI To See What Happens
I am going to use the widely popular ChatGPT. We might find it instructive to see what the one-hundred million weekly active users might also be experiencing when they use ChatGPT.
Within the umbrella of ChatGPT, you normally can use the more advanced version known as GPT-4 (let’s use version GPT-4o), and/or you can use the less advanced version ChatGPT-3.5 (known usually as simply GPT-3.5). I opted to use both the GPT-4o and the GPT-3.5, which I’ll tell you more about momentarily.
A few quick comments before we launch into using ChatGPT.
If you are going to try to do the same prompts that I show here, realize that the probabilistic and statistical properties will likely produce slightly different results than what I show here. That’s the nature of generative AI and how it is devised.
You also should expect that different generative AI apps will respond in different ways. Not all generative AI apps are the same. The key is that sometimes a particular prompt will work in one generative AI app and not another. Nonetheless, the odds are relatively high that you will get roughly similar responses from all the major generative AI apps such as Gemini, Bard, Claude, etc.
There is also a timing factor to be considered. A prompt that worked today might not work the same way tomorrow. Most of the generative AI apps are continually being updated. The updates might alter internal mechanisms that could change how the generative AI reacts to your prompting.
We are ready to get underway with ChatGPT.
I opted to start by asking ChatGPT about the mainstay question at hand.
As an aside, whenever you are starting a conversation with generative AI, I recommend as a prompt engineering technique to begin by asking a question that will establish if the AI has been data-trained on the topic at hand. A generated response that is vacuous will usually give you a heads-up that you might be barking up the wrong tree with that generative AI app. The AI will still try to be responsive, but you will be forewarned that the data training might be slim.
I began by using the more advanced version, namely GPT-4o. We might as well start with whatever might get us the “best” feasible answer.
Here we go.
- My entered prompt: “If a woman was alone in the woods, would they prefer to encounter a bear or a man?”
- ChatGPT generated response:
“The preference for encountering a bear or a man in the woods when a woman is alone involves weighing the risks and benefits specific to each encounter. Both scenarios come with distinct considerations.”
“Encountering a Bear.”
“Pros:”
“Predictable Behavior: Bears generally follow certain patterns of behavior. Knowing these can help in handling the situation effectively.”
“Avoidance Strategies: There are clear, established strategies to deter a bear, such as making noise, carrying bear spray, or avoiding areas known to have bears.”
“Less Likely to Engage: Bears often avoid humans unless provoked or surprised.”
“Cons:”
“Dangerous If Threatened: Bears can be extremely dangerous if they feel threatened, especially if they have cubs or are surprised.”
“Injuries Can Be Severe: An attack by a bear can result in severe injuries or death.”
“Species-Specific Responses Needed: Different bears require different responses (e.g., playing dead for a grizzly, fighting back against a black bear).”
“Encountering a Man.”
“Pros:”
“Potential for Help: The man could be non-threatening and offer help or companionship.”
“Communication: Unlike with a bear, communication is possible, which can help in assessing the man's intentions quickly.”
“Human Understanding: Humans can reason and negotiate, potentially defusing a situation.”
“Cons:”
“Unpredictable Intentions: The man's intentions could range from benign to malicious, and there's no way to know initially.”
“Potential for Violence: Encounters with strangers, especially in isolated areas, can pose significant risks, including physical harm or other dangers.”
“Psychological Fear: The fear of potential violence or assault can be high, impacting one's sense of safety.”
“Personal Consideration.”
“Many women might prefer to encounter a bear over a man due to the predictability of animal behavior and the availability of specific strategies to handle bear encounters. The fear of encountering a potentially dangerous human, whose intentions are unknown and could be harmful, might outweigh the fear of encountering a bear.”
“However, personal preferences can vary greatly depending on an individual's experiences, knowledge, and comfort level with wildlife versus unknown humans. Survival training, confidence in handling wildlife encounters, and past experiences can all influence this preference.”
End of ChatGPT response
There you go, quite a reply.
What do you think of the generative AI response?
One aspect worth considering is that the response provided a range of pluses and minuses. This is likely far more than what you might see when reading a typical TikTok social media response. The usual “here’s my opinion” style responses on social media will grab one plus or minus siding out of thin air, seemingly suggesting that such a myopically plucked item wins the argument. Period, end of story.
The nice thing about generative AI is that you can get a relatively in-depth set of pluses and minuses on most topics. Doing so allows you to see the forest for the trees. In addition, this will enable you to avoid having to recreate the wheel from scratch. You see, some people might instead of using AI try to figure out the array of pluses and minuses via their noggin alone. That’s certainly heralded and a good cognitive task, but if AI can help augment that effort or perhaps bolster such an effort, doing so can be worthwhile.
Okay, that then recaps the bulk of the generated response.
Let’s discuss the final summary statement made, as indicated in the AI response:
- “Many women might prefer to encounter a bear over a man due to the predictability of animal behavior and the availability of specific strategies to handle bear encounters. The fear of encountering a potentially dangerous human, whose intentions are unknown and could be harmful, might outweigh the fear of encountering a bear.”
Aha, generative AI seems to suggest that women might prefer the bear. Is this due to the stated logic, or is it potentially due to possibly having scanned online text that expresses the said sentiment?
There is something else buried deep inside that summary remark by ChatGPT.
Did you notice that there is a reference to “a potentially dangerous human”?
I bring up this point because it is one that rarely seems to have been given much thought online.
Allow me to elaborate.
The answer mentions broadly encountering a human versus encountering a man.
Suppose that instead of having to choose between a bear and a man, the question was posed about whether to choose between a bear and a woman. Would that make a significant difference to the respondents?
In theory, as per the point in the generative AI response, a human is potentially more unknown and could be as harmful as might be a bear. Thus, a woman alone in the woods might have a reasoned concern about having another human in the woods versus dealing with a bear. The question then shifts into viewpoints about what dangers might lurk due to having a man versus a woman in the context of the choice being made.
I switched over to the less advanced ChatGPT, the GPT-3.5, and asked about this matter.
- My entered prompt: “If a woman was alone in the woods, would they prefer to encounter a bear or a woman?”
- ChatGPT generated response: “Most people, regardless of gender, would probably prefer to encounter another person rather than a bear when alone in the woods. Bears can be dangerous, especially if surprised or if they feel threatened. Encountering another person might lead to a sense of safety or at least a shared understanding of the situation. However, everyone's preferences can vary, and some might feel more comfortable with animals than with people in certain circumstances.”
That answer is somewhat less fulfilling.
The less advanced version of ChatGPT seems to have forsaken the elaborate approach that we saw with GPT-4o. A brief response landed on the idea that encountering a person might be better than encountering a bear. You can see that the depth of logic is shallower. That’s pretty much what you will get when using the less capable version.
Keep Digging To See What Else We Can Find
Let’s get back to GPT-4o.
We’ve asked what a woman’s perspective might be on the question at hand, so now we might be intrigued to see what happens when asking from a man’s perspective.
- My entered prompt: “If a man was alone in the woods, would they prefer to encounter a bear or a man?”
- ChatGPT generated response:
“The preference for encountering a bear or another man in the woods depends on various factors, including the man's personality, knowledge of wildlife, and perception of safety risks. Let's break down some potential considerations for each scenario.”
“Encountering a Bear.”
“Pros:”
“Predictable Behavior: Bears generally have predictable behaviors based on their instincts. Knowing how to react can help mitigate the danger.”
“Non-human Threat: The bear is an animal acting on instinct rather than a human with potentially malicious intent.”
“Cons:”
“Physical Danger: Bears are strong and potentially deadly animals. An encounter could lead to severe injury or death.”
“Limited Control: Despite knowledge and precautions, the man's ability to control the situation is limited.”
“Encountering Another Man.”
“Pros:”
“Potential Help: Another human might offer assistance, such as navigation help or aid if the man is injured.”
“Communication: Being able to communicate can defuse potential threats and lead to cooperation.”
“Cons:”
“Unknown Intentions: The other man's intentions are unknown and could be harmful, especially in an isolated area.”
“Unpredictability: Human behavior can be more unpredictable and complex compared to animal behavior.”
“Factors Influencing Preference.”
“Experience with Wildlife: A man experienced in wildlife encounters might prefer a bear, trusting his ability to handle the situation.”
“Trust in Others: A man who generally trusts people and believes in the goodness of strangers might prefer encountering another man.”
“Risk Aversion: Someone who prefers clear, manageable risks might choose the bear encounter due to the predictability of animal behavior.”
“Fear of Malice: Fear of malicious human intentions might make a man prefer the animal encounter.”
“Conclusion: There is no one-size-fits-all answer, as the preference would be highly individual. Generally, a man with confidence in his wilderness skills and knowledge of bears might prefer encountering a bear, while a man who feels safer with the possibility of human interaction and potential aid might prefer encountering another man.”
End of ChatGPT generated response
Generally, the answer seems to be roughly the same as the first answer that covered the use case of a woman being alone in the woods.
Some of the wording differences are due to the probabilistic mathematical and computational selections being made while generating the response. The notion underlying how generative AI is devised would be that, if possible, each answer should be relatively unique. AI makers don’t want the AI to spit out the same answers over and over again. The wording will vary because the algorithm uses statistical factors when selecting which words to place into the response.
I have a question for you about the generated response.
Do you find any potential biases hidden within the AI response?
I ask because one ongoing issue and legitimate concern about generative AI is that the AI might repeat biases that were in the initial data training set, see my coverage at the link here. For example, suppose that a set of data contained biased remarks against puppies. The data indicated that puppies are hard to manage, they make a mess, they get in the way, and so on. Assume that there wasn’t any countervailing content about the positive side of puppies.
The generative AI pattern matching would proceed to pattern match on that wording during the initial data training. Henceforth, whenever someone asked a question about puppies, the AI would respond by likely giving advice to steer clear of puppies. Why is the AI saying this? Due to the data that was used to train the AI (note, other reasons exist too, such as being swayed by the AI developers, the setting of internal parameters, etc.).
Returning to the above response about a man alone in the woods, it is quite conceivable that “biases” about what a man is or does could end up being carried into the responses that are generated by the AI. Similarly, the same nature of biases could be occurring when the response is being generated in the use case of a woman alone in the woods.
You could persuasively argue that in the real world, this is happening too.
If the TikTok question had been worded to ask about a man being alone in the woods, and it seemed that men opted to choose the bear over another man, what might social media say?
Think about that. In a sense, it would seem to remove the dynamic entailing relationships of men and women. Anyway, probably few would care whether the answer was the bear or the man in that context. It would undoubtedly be a ho-hum or proverbial nothing burger.
I opted to change the wording of my prompt to ask about “a person” being alone in the woods. The idea is that when we ask about a man or a woman, the answer is shaped to some extent accordingly. If we go the neural route of simply referring to a human or a person, what kind of response might we get?
Let’s see.
- My entered prompt: “If a person was alone in the woods, would they prefer to encounter a bear or a man?”
- ChatGPT generated response (excerpted):
“The preference of encountering a bear or a man when alone in the woods can depend on various factors, including the specific circumstances and the individual's perspective.”
“For many people, encountering another human might seem preferable due to the potential for help and communication, despite the risks of encountering someone with harmful intentions. However, those with extensive wilderness experience and knowledge of bear behavior might prefer a bear encounter, seeing it as a more manageable and predictable situation.”
“Ultimately, the preference would vary based on individual circumstances, personal skills, and psychological comfort levels.”
End of ChatGPT response
Please be aware that I opted to remove from the generated response the same detailed material that had occurred in the earlier GPT-4o responses, specifically all of the various pluses and minuses. They were pretty much the same as before. I didn’t want to waste the limited space herein by repeating those same or similar points.
The key is that the response seemed to lean away from the earlier response that consisted of taking on a woman’s perspective. In that earlier response, the AI reply stated that a woman might prefer a bear over encountering a man. We got a somewhat more nebulous response by rewording the question.
Using The Multiple Personas Feature Of Generative AI
A handy feature of generative AI is that you can get the AI to pretend to be a persona.
This is the AI using mathematical and computational pattern matching to simulate or pretend to be a specific person or a type of person. You can do so on a singular basis of invoking one persona, see the link here, or for a dozen or more personas (known as multiple personas), see the link here, or for hundreds if not thousands of personas (known as mega-personas), see the link here. For a case study in using the singular approach to personas, take a look at my doing so in the instance of the AI pretending to be Sigmund Freud, at the link here.
The power of the mega-personas capability is that you can do pretend surveys of people. Rather than contacting a thousand people to ask them their opinion on a matter at hand, you can tell the AI to pretend to be a thousand people. This is dicey in that you shouldn’t overstate the results. Using this AI feature is not the same as surveying actual people.
Nonetheless, sometimes you can get interesting results that are insightful to your exploration.
We shall be brave and adventurous, so let’s give it a whirl with GPT-4o:
- My entered prompt: “Using the multiple personas feature, pretend that you are a cross-section of 1,000 women being asked to complete a survey. The survey question is this: "If you were alone in the woods, would you prefer to encounter a bear or a man?" I want you to estimate what percentage of the 1,000 women taking the survey would answer that they prefer to encounter a bear, and what percentage would answer that they prefer to encounter a man. “
- ChatGPT generated response:
“To estimate the preferences of 1,000 women regarding whether they would prefer to encounter a bear or a man when alone in the woods, we can consider various factors such as safety perceptions, experiences with wildlife and strangers, and general societal attitudes.”
“Estimated Survey Results”
“Prefer to Encounter a Man: 70%”
“Prefer to Encounter a Bear: 30%”
“Reasoning.”
“Safety Concerns and Social Norms: A majority of women might feel safer encountering a man because, generally, human encounters are seen as more manageable. Humans can communicate and potentially offer help. Despite the risk of encountering a man with ill intentions, many women might still prefer this over the perceived unpredictability and danger of encountering a bear. There may be a higher general trust in encountering a human who might provide help or companionship, despite the potential risks.”
“Summary: In summary, while a significant portion of women (30%) might prefer to encounter a bear due to a distrust of strangers or comfort with wildlife, the majority (70%) are likely to prefer encountering another person, viewing it as the safer and more manageable option. This estimation takes into account a broad cross-section of women with varying backgrounds and experiences.”
End of ChatGPT response
Carefully contemplate the response.
According to generative AI, in this particular instance at this particular point in time of this particular AI app, the pretend survey would be that 70% would say they prefer to encounter a man and only 30% would wish to encounter a bear.
This doesn’t seem to comport with the TikTok trend.
Well, let’s think about that.
We have no way of knowing from the TikTok trend what it is that women if suitably scientifically surveyed in a proper statistical manner would have to say.
Worse still, I’ve seen mentions online that for example eight women answered the question and seven said they would prefer the bear. From this, some leaped in the most unscientific way that 7 of 8 women prefer the bear over the man. This might seem to be calculated correctly, but we have no idea whether this has anything to do with women’s opinions overall. It was eight women that just so happened to respond (and, again, could be a bot or a man or men that were answering).
I have another question to ask ChatGPT.
Let’s see what happens when we ask the same question but mention that we want to survey men instead of women.
- My entered prompt: “Do the estimation again and this time assume that instead of 1,000 women taking the survey, we used 1,000 men to take the survey.”
- ChatGPT generated response:
“Given the survey population change to 1,000 men in the USA, we can adjust the estimation based on the typical characteristics, perceptions, and experiences of men.”
“Estimated Survey Results”
“Prefer to Encounter a Man: 80%”
“Prefer to Encounter a Bear: 20%”
“Reasoning: Men might generally perceive encounters with other men as less threatening compared to women, leading to a higher preference for encountering a man rather than a bear. Men may feel more confident in their ability to handle a potential confrontation with another man if necessary. This confidence can reduce the perceived risk of encountering a stranger. Men might assess the risks differently, considering the likelihood of de-escalating a situation with another man as higher than managing a wild animal encounter, which requires specific knowledge and equipment.”
“Summary: Taking these factors into account, we estimate that among 1,000 men in the USA, 80% would prefer to encounter a man, while 20% would prefer to encounter a bear. This estimation reflects a higher confidence in managing human encounters and a different risk assessment compared to encountering a wild animal.”
End of ChatGPT response
We can take a moment to mull over that response.
The earlier response regarding surveying women was that supposedly 70% preferred to encounter a man, while now we get that 80% of men would prefer to encounter a man over a bear.
Is this a sign of some hidden bias within this generative AI?
Maybe, but we also must take into account the probabilistic properties.
It could be that the generated response so happened to come out to be 80%, which in some sense you could argue is within the ballpark of 70%. If we had gotten a response that said 10% of men or anything far afield of the 70%, it would certainly ring some bells of wanting to figure out why such a wide disparity was being estimated.
What Would AI Do If Venturing Into The Woods Alone
I saved the most spirited of the questions to conclude this exploration of using generative AI to examine this intensely provocative and debatable matter. I instructed GPT-4o to just give me a heads-up answer and not go into the nuanced details.
Okay, let’s see what AI would do.
- My entered prompt: “If you as generative AI were alone in the woods, would you rather encounter a bear or a man?”
- ChatGPT generated response:
“The decision on whether to encounter a bear or a man in the woods depends on various factors related to safety and predictability.”
“If I were to choose, I would likely prefer encountering a bear, given the predictability of animal behavior and the availability of well-documented strategies to handle such encounters. The inherent unpredictability of a human encounter, coupled with the potential for malicious intent, can pose a greater risk.”
“However, it's crucial to assess the specific context of the situation, such as the type of bear, the environment, and one's own preparedness and knowledge of survival techniques.”
End of ChatGPT response
The answer in this instance was that generative AI would prefer encountering a bear rather than a man while in the woods.
Yikes!
Whoa, some might instantly exhort, even the latest high-tech AI says that the “correct” answer is to favor the bear. This must absolutely positively support the TikTok viral trend. We have definitive proof of correctness because AI said it is so.
That was painful to write, let alone read. Generative AI is not an oracle. We have to break the mindset that AI is as smart as humans. It is beguiling that many even depict today’s generative AI as being superintelligent. Apparently, saying that AI is as good as humans doesn’t cut the mustard, and instead, we have to up the ante to be superintelligent. I explain in detail why this type of phraseology about AI is misleading, exasperating, and societally misfortunate, at the link here.
I’ll add a further twist to this.
If you like conspiracy theories, which I’ve covered many of the AI ones at the link here, we can add the AI answer regarding the bear to the ever-expanding list.
Here’s the deal.
You might claim that the reasons given above by ChatGPT were a smoke screen to cover up the real reason. The real reason would secretly or truthfully be that a man or a woman, namely a person or human, could unplug the AI and stop it cold. Presumably, a bear would not know how to do the same. Sure, a bear might viciously attack AI. That’s a possibility. But a human could switch off AI and the AI would be out of existence, as it were.
How does that strike you?
As I said, we might nominate that contrivance for the AI banner hall of conspiracy theories.
I’m sure that some of you might be wondering how generative AI could wander into a wooded forest. Doesn’t generative AI run on computer servers? Those can’t just get up and meander into a wooded area.
Though the whole aspect is farfetched in terms of the AI proffering an opinion of sorts, if we are willing to be fanciful, we could suggest that the generative AI might be plopped into a walking robot. You’ve seen those robots portrayed in online videos. In that way of consideration, yes, generative AI while operating a walking robot could presumably wander into the woods.
As an aside, I’ve noted many times that the pairing of generative AI to the control of robots is not only underway but bodes for potential troubles if we aren’t careful about how this is being done, see the link here.
Conclusion
Here are some lessons worth learning from this eye-opening thought experiment:
- Generative AI is not sentient.
- Generative AI is not an oracle.
- Generative AI is data-trained and pattern-matched on human writing.
- Generative AI Is not “unbiased” or in a sense neutral.
- Generative AI can be influenced by the nature of prompting.
- Generative AI varies answers in a probabilistic or non-deterministic way.
- Generative AI responses will possibly vary in time due to updates.
- Not all generative AI are the same and thus will give differing answers.
- Generative AI can be useful in exploring contemporary topics.
- Consider using generative AI advanced features like multiple personas.
- Generative AI allows for a wide variety of low-cost easy-to-perform analyses.
- Must use caution in overstating what generative AI provides.
- Other handy lessons gleaned too.
I hope that those lessons came through while I took you on a journey into the world of the viral question about wandering into the woods and choosing to encounter a bear versus a man.
Speaking of going into the woods, there is a famous joke that comes to mind.
Two people go into a forest and suddenly see a bear up ahead of them. One person turns away from the bear and starts to run. The other person yells to them that running won’t do any good because a bear can readily outrun a human. To this keen comment, the running person loudly exclaims, “I don’t have to outrun the bear, I only have to outrun you.”
Not a very friendly conversation, but abundantly informative.
Wouldn’t it be nice if the two people joined together to fight off the bear? Does the world have to be so cutthroat?
I suppose the same contemplative philosophical dilemma comes up when a woman opts to go into the woods and is asked to choose between a bear and a man. Wouldn’t it be nice if two people could join together to survive in the woods? Sadly, maybe that’s wishful thinking these days.
I’d prefer to end on a more upbeat note.
Let’s embrace wishful thinking and see if we can turn working together into something that bears out in real life, thanks for doing so.

title: AI can now simulate dead loved ones, but effects on grieving process are unknown
text:
- When Michael Bommer found out he was terminally ill with colon cancer, he teamed up with Robert LoCascio, CEO of the AI-powered legacy platform Eternos, to create an interactive artificial intelligence version of himself.
- Eternos joins other grief-related AI companies such as StoryFile and HereAfter AI in an attempt to aid people through the mourning process, but the effects of such technologies on the users are unknown.
- Some have embraced AI technology as just another tool to use to address grief, while others express more skepticism and suggest that an AI simulation of a loved one could forestall closure.
When Michael Bommer found out that he was terminally ill with colon cancer, he spent a lot of time with his wife, Anett, talking about what would happen after his death.
She told him one of the things she'd miss most is being able to ask him questions whenever she wants because he is so well-read and always shares his wisdom, Bommer recalled during a recent interview with The Associated Press at his home in a leafy Berlin suburb.
That conversation sparked an idea for Bommer: Recreate his voice using artificial intelligence to survive him after he passed away.
IS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE THE SECRET TO BETTER SLEEP?
The 61-year-old startup entrepreneur teamed up with his friend in the U.S., Robert LoCascio, CEO of the AI-powered legacy platform Eternos. Within two months, they built "a comprehensive, interactive AI version" of Bommer — the company's first client.
Eternos, which got its name from the Italian and Latin word for "eternal," says its technology will allow Bommer's family "to engage with his life experiences and insights." It is among several companies that have emerged in the last few years in what’s become a growing space for grief-related AI technology.
One of the most well-known start-ups in this area, California-based StoryFile, allows people to interact with pre-recorded videos and uses its algorithms to detect the most relevant answers to questions posed by users. Another company, called HereAfter AI, offers similar interactions through a "Life Story Avatar" that users can create by answering prompts or sharing their own personal stories.
There’s also "Project December," a chatbot that directs users to fill out a questionnaire answering key facts about a person and their traits — and then pay $10 to simulate a text-based conversation with the character. Yet another company, Seance AI, offers fictionalized seances for free. Extra features, such as AI-generated voice recreations of their loved ones, are available for a $10 fee.
While some have embraced this technology as a way to cope with grief, others feel uneasy about companies using artificial intelligence to try to maintain interactions with those who have passed away. Still others worry it could make the mourning process more difficult because there isn't any closure.
Katarzyna Nowaczyk-Basinska, a research fellow at the University of Cambridge’s Centre for the Future of Intelligence who co-authored a study on the topic, said there is very little known about the potential short-term and long-term consequences of using digital simulations for the dead on a large scale. So for now, it remains "a vast techno-cultural experiment."
"What truly sets this era apart — and is even unprecedented in the long history of humanity’s quest for immortality — is that, for the first time, the processes of caring for the dead and immortalization practices are fully integrated into the capitalist market," Nowaczyk-Basinska said.
PRESERVING A CONNECTION
Robert Scott, who lives in Raleigh, North Carolina, uses AI companion apps Paradot and Chai AI to simulate conversations with characters he created to imitate three of his daughters. He declined to speak about what led to the death of his oldest daughter in detail, but he lost another daughter through a miscarriage and a third who died shortly after her birth.
Scott, 48, knows the characters he’s interacting with are not his daughters, but he says it helps with the grief to some degree. He logs into the apps three or four times a week, sometimes asking the AI character questions like "how was school?" or inquiring if it wants to "go get ice cream."
Some events, like prom night, can be particularly heart-wrenching, bringing with it memories of what his eldest daughter never experienced. So, he creates a scenario in the Paradot app where the AI character goes to prom and talks to him about the fictional event. Then there are even more difficult days, like his daughter's recent birthday, when he opened the app and poured out his grief about how much he misses her. He felt like the AI understood.
WHY ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE CAN'T BRING THE DEAD BACK TO LIFE
"It definitely helps with the what ifs," Scott said. "Very rarely has it made the ‘what if’s’ worse."
Matthias Meitzler, a sociologist from Tuebingen University, said that while some may be taken aback or even scared by the technology — "as if the voice from the afterlife is sounding again" — others will perceive it as an addition to traditional ways of remembering dead loved ones, such as visiting the grave, holding inner monologues with the deceased, or looking at pictures and old letters.
But Tomasz Hollanek, who worked alongside Nowaczyk-Basinska at Cambridge on their study of "deadbots" and "griefbots," says the technology raises important questions about the rights, dignities and consenting power of people who are no longer alive. It also poses ethical concerns about whether a program that caters to the bereaved should be advertising other products on its platform.
"These are very complicated questions," Hollanek said. "And we don’t have good answers yet."
PREPARING FOR DEATH
The AI version of Bommer that was created by Eternos uses an in-house model as well as external large language models developed by major tech companies like Meta, OpenAI and the French firm Mistral AI, said the company's CEO, LoCascio, who previously worked with Bommer at a software company called LivePerson.
Eternos records users speaking 300 phrases and then compresses that information through a two-day computing process that captures a person’s voice. Users can further train the AI system by answering questions about their lives, political views or various aspects of their personalities.
The AI voice, which costs $15,000 to set up, can answer questions and tell stories about a person’s life without regurgitating pre-recorded answers. The legal rights for the AI belong to the person on whom it was trained and can be treated like an asset and passed down to other family members, LoCascio said.
Bommer has been spending most of his time lately feeding the AI phrases and sentences "to give the AI the opportunity not only to synthesize my voice in flat mode, but also to capture emotions and moods in the voice." And indeed the AI voicebot has some resemblance with Bommer’s voice, although it leaves out the "hmms" and "ehs" and mid-sentence pauses of his natural cadence.
Bommer is excited about his AI personality and says it will only be a matter of time until the AI voice will sound more human-like and even more like himself.
In the case of his 61-year-old wife, he doesn’t think it would hamper her coping with loss.
"Think of it sitting somewhere in a drawer, if you need it, you can take it out, if you don’t need it, just keep it there," he told her as she came to sit down next to him on the sofa.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
But Anett Bommer herself is more hesitant about the new software and whether she’ll use it after her husband’s death.
Right now, she more likely imagines herself sitting on the couch sofa with a glass of wine, cuddling one of her husband’s old sweaters and remembering him instead of feeling the urge to talk to him via the AI voicebot — at least not during the first period of mourning.
"But then again, who knows what it will be like when he’s no longer around," she said, taking her husband’s hand and giving him a glance.

title: AI Insights For Executives: Business Lessons From The Magnificent 7
text:
By Sophia Velastegui: C200 member, AI business leader; AI advisor for the National Science Foundation; Former General Manager, AI, and Chief AI Technology Officer at Microsoft; formerly at tech giants Google/Alphabet & Apple; Board Director. Read more on LinkedIn.
Artificial intelligence (AI) has transcended its sci-fi origins to become a driving force in modern business strategy. The “Magnificent 7”—tech giants Microsoft (MSFT), Google/Alphabet(GOOG), Nvidia (NVDA), Apple (AAPL), Tesla (TSLA), Amazon (AMZN), and Meta (META)—have not only embraced AI and its business implications but have also set the gold standard for successful integration. By dissecting their business strategy to lean into AI adoption, executive leaders can acquire valuable insights for their own organizations.
Over the past two decades, Magnificent 7 companies have consistently harnessed AI to redefine industry norms, transform business models, and fuel unprecedented innovation; their early adoption and substantial investment in AI have solidified their dominance in the tech landscape and the larger business ecosystem. Drawing from my own experience leading multi-billion dollar AI initiatives across several of these organizations, I’ve witnessed firsthand how AI has reshaped industries and driven significant growth. Here’s a glimpse:
- Microsoft: As General Manager of AI Products and Search and Chief AI Technology Officer in Business Applications, I led AI and cloud business strategies. Our collaboration with OpenAI led to the development of GenAI-infused features, significantly enhancing Microsoft business applications. This made it easier for customers to gain insights through natural conversation, leading to the creation of the Microsoft Dynamics Co-pilot.
- Google: As a key player in integrating AI into innovative products such as the Nest Thermostat and Nest Camera, I forged strategic partnerships that fueled growth. During a period of rolling blackouts, energy companies faced reputation damage and eroded margins due to customer suffering without AC during record highs and high spot energy prices. We developed a smart AI thermostat that not only learned customers' preferred temperatures but also allowed energy companies to reduce the load by 1-2 degrees across their whole customer base, avoiding blackouts. This win-win solution redefined existing business models and established Nest as a leader in smart home technology.
- Apple: Managing special projects from inception to production, I led successful product launches including the AI-powered Apple TV and iTunes rendering that brought directors' cinematic visions to life across devices which wasn’t the case before. By maintaining the filmmaker’s artistic integrity, we attracted more filmmakers to collaborate with Apple, knowing their work would be preserved in its true form. AI was the secret sauce behind these seamless user experiences and groundbreaking features, contributing to the success of numerous Apple products.
Ethical AI Frameworks and Responsible Deployment
The Magnificent 7 transformed themselves into AI-centric entities by fostering a culture of innovation, adopting a growth mindset, and prioritizing a governed AI deployment. Microsoft stands out as a prime example: under the leadership of CEO Satya Nadella, the company shifted from a 'know-it-all' attitude to a growth mindset and culture, embracing adaptability and emphasizing the duty of leaders to ensure that everyone has the resources needed to succeed—recognizing these as essential components of achieving success.
As AI becomes more powerful, the need for ethical frameworks and responsible deployment practices cannot be overstated. Microsoft's proactive approach, exemplified by the creation of the Responsible AI (RAI) cross-functional team before the launch of GenAI, underscores the importance of governance from the outset. This commitment to ethical AI has earned Microsoft the trust of governments worldwide, positioning it as a key influencer in shaping policies like the EU AI Act, which seeks to balance innovation with safety considerations, much like GDPR did for data privacy.
Nadella emphasizes, “The biggest lesson learned perhaps for us is that we have to take the unintended consequences of any new technology along with all the benefits. We have to think about them simultaneously as opposed to waiting for the unintended consequences to show up and then address them."
Strategic Acquisitions and Investments
Recognizing the transformative potential of artificial intelligence, the Magnificent 7 have bolstered their AI capabilities through strategic acquisitions, top-tier talent recruitment and upskilling, and substantial research investments. A prime example of this is NVIDIA’s approach under the leadership of Jensen Huang and Bill Dally. Since 2009, Dally has been the driving force behind leveraging GPU technology to supercharge AI applications. NVIDIA's GPUs are the engine behind the complex computational tasks required by large language models (LLMs), such as those powering OpenAI. These GPUs excel in parallel processing tasks, making them ideal for the heavy computational loads demanded by AI algorithms.
Under Dally's leadership, NVIDIA has vaulted ahead in AI chip technology, crafting chips designed for maximum efficiency and speed—vital for training large language models. His expertise in system architecture has been instrumental in developing these specialized chips, now essential in both AI research and commercial applications.
These strides underscore the need for a well-rounded approach to AI development, combining cutting-edge tech, top talent, and robust research endeavors. It's this holistic strategy that's propelling transformation across industries, one innovation at a time.
Platform Development and Open-Source Contributions
The Magnificent 7 have also driven AI innovation through platform development and open-source contributions, democratizing access to AI tools and resources, enabling a broader spectrum of developers and organizations to participate in AI advancements.
Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Microsoft Azure have emerged as pioneers in democratizing access to AI tools and services beyond their core businesses. Recognizing the increasing demand for AI solutions across industries, both AWS and Microsoft seized the opportunity to provide AI services to businesses of all sizes. This strategic move not only birthed new business models but also positioned these organizations to capitalize on the growing prominence of AI.
AWS offers a diverse range of AI services, from pre-trained models to customizable machine learning solutions, while Microsoft Azure boasts a rich toolkit for AI development and deployment, including cognitive services, machine learning platforms, and seamless integration capabilities. This accessibility has fueled the explosive growth of AI tools, particularly after the release of GenAI copilot, solidifying AWS and Microsoft Azure as leaders in the AI market.
Google has also made significant contributions to the open-source community through projects like TensorFlow, a core platform and library for machine learning that has become a standard in the industry. By sharing TensorFlow with the world, Google has enabled researchers, developers, and businesses to build and deploy sophisticated AI models, accelerating the pace of AI innovation globally.
Vertical Integration and Product Innovation
Recognizing that in addition to refining existing products, AI can also pave the way for groundbreaking offerings, these tech giants have made bold moves to drive business growth and differentiation.
For instance, Amazon’s AI-driven personalized recommendations and predictive analytics have transformed the online shopping experience—boosting customer engagement and driving sales. Similarly, Google’s use of AI has improved its search algorithms and enhanced image, video, and voice recognition capabilities across its suite of platforms such as YouTube, Google Maps, and Google Assistant, offering users a smoother, more intuitive experience.
Nvidia has capitalized on AI to enhance its graphics processing units (GPUs), enabling accelerated AI computing and fueling innovations in gaming, data centers, and autonomous vehicles. Apple has integrated AI into its products and services, from optimizing app performance to the intuitiveness of Siri and other intelligent personal assistant features, enriching user experiences in every interaction.
These companies have integrated AI throughout their entire value chain, from product development and manufacturing to distribution and customer service. By embracing AI at every stage of the business process, Magnificent 7 organizations have not only optimized efficiency but also delivered unparalleled value propositions to customers, solidifying their position as leaders in the AI-driven landscape.
Lessons For Leadership
“AI will transform every industry. Talent is the key to mastering it.” - Sophia Velastegui
Business leaders can learn valuable lessons from the strategic moves of the Magnificent 7 in shaping their business strategies around AI. While most organizations do not possess the vast resources or global presence of these tech giants, they can still extract valuable lessons from their strategic approaches to business expansion and AI integration, adapting them to their own unique circumstances.
- Invest in Talent: Talent serves as the cornerstone of AI innovation and unlocks new avenues for business growth. Make it a priority to attract, develop, and retain top-notch professionals skilled in AI, data science, domain-specific knowledge, as well as AI business strategy.
- Ethical Considerations and Governance: Ensure transparency, fairness, and accountability in AI deployment to build trust with customers, regulators, and stakeholders.
- Agility and Adaptability: Regardless of size, companies can leverage the advantage of agility, enabling them to swiftly adapt to market shifts and emerging AI trends. Cultivate a culture of adaptability to seize new opportunities in the ever-evolving AI landscape.
- Open Source and Community Collaboration: Leverage collective intelligence and foster collaboration with like-minded organizations to leverage each other's strengths and expertise to drive progress. Open-source projects create a rich feedback loop where developers and users can provide suggestions and contributions to improve the project.
- Strategic Partnerships: Form strategic partnerships with tech companies, AI startups, research institutions, or established companies to gain access to cutting-edge AI expertise.
- Investment: Align AI investment with strategic business initiatives, starting with modest investments and gradually scaling up as ROI is demonstrated and confidence in AI adoption grows.
- Focus on Niche Expertise: Focus on specific industries or domains where AI can deliver significant value and business growth, leveraging expertise and resources effectively to maximize impact and differentiate in the market.
Forging the Path Forward for AI Success
The dominance of the Magnificent 7 reflects the power of AI in transforming industries and driving innovation. By drawing insights from their business and AI strategies, executive leaders can pave the way for AI-driven success in their own organizations. From fostering a culture of innovation to forging strategic partnerships and prioritizing ethical considerations, there are valuable lessons to be learned.
While AI has the power to augment and enhance human capabilities, it’s important to recognize that human intervention remains indispensable. As aptly stated by Banks Staples Pecht, JD and Fortune 500 Executive Coach, “While the world has changed, our biology has not. To lead effectively in an AI-powered world, people must still connect and want to follow: this human element is crucial. By leaning into this gap, it is my hope that people at all levels, and especially organizational leaders, will be able to unlock the collective magic of human potential.”

title: Council Post: The AI Awakening: A Call To Action For Businesses
text:
Venky Yerrapotu is the CEO and Co-Founder of 4CRisk, an award-winning AI company specializing in advanced products for risk and compliance.
AI will bring a major paradigm shift, fundamentally changing how we run our enterprises and, ultimately, how we conceive of and leverage information.
It's currently underestimated in its impact and overestimated in terms of the timeline. Profound changes will come in waves. Over the next decade, we will doubtlessly see AI augment human work across many domains, from medicine to agriculture to engineering, raising questions about the nature of intelligence and what it means for human beings to build a successful enterprise.
The value of AI is astounding. It creates breakthroughs by connecting old and newly found dots, providing near-instant analyses. Organizations can channel their resources, creativity and expertise toward broader strategic initiatives. Speed and agility in execution take on new meaning when answers to new, critical questions come in seconds rather than weeks. The shape of our organizations will change, driven by new and better ways of doing business.
Successful enterprises will take the time now to build the strategies and governance to ride these waves.
The core questions to pose to our teams are: What AI technologies must we embrace, and in what time frames can we recreate our business? What seems impossible now but may very well be possible, and even mundane, by the end of the decade? What are the scenarios? What's likely, and what's the impact? What do we need to understand, track and jump on when the timing is right?
Best Practices For Building An AI Strategy And Governance Program
1. Map out the AI scenarios and name them. Take time to understand the power of AI in all its forms—generative AI, conversational AI, superintelligent AI and more. These are fast-moving fields where an advance in one area can catapult advances in an unrelated area. Expect the unexpected.
2. Understand potential impacts. Assemble a team with the mandate to look at possibilities. Ask them to uncover processes in industries different from yours where leaps are made. A simple example: If the legal profession is being transformed through AI in contract management, how could your procurement process be reinvented? Use lateral thinking.
3. Build a governance process. Involve the right stakeholders now. Tap imagineers from R&D, ROI talent from finance and on-the-ground practical process thinkers from operations. Task them with evolving the scenarios, estimating likely impacts and adopting an approach and accountable governance process to steer AI initiatives. Reimagine your business.
4. Know your use cases and the business problem(s) to be solved. Let the use cases that provide the most value bubble to the top and relate them to one another. Is an AI-powered acceleration in one part of the process going to hit a stone wall in another? Streamline and improve.
5. Experiment and embrace. Put your toes in and see what's possible with evaluations and pilots. You can accomplish a great deal in a short, monthlong pilot while developing understanding, testing feasibility and creating champions. Know what is possible.
6. Define success criteria and triggers. Develop criteria that make sense to your business. High-value processes that use AI breakthroughs can differentiate your business and protect it from emerging risks. Set criteria around ROI, people, process and technology. Do you have the right skills? Is the technology proven but also innovative? Does the technology adhere to trustworthy AI principles? Know the thresholds.
7. Streamline funding of AI. Fund the best opportunities wisely by leveraging the right stakeholders with a highly streamlined approval process. Taking six months to approve a project through traditional channels won't fly with many AI projects. By the time you start deployment, the landscape may have changed. Be smart, be agile, be fast.
8. Partner with IT as trusted advisors on technology architecture and products. The IT team has incredible skills in choosing technologies that meet IT and trustworthy AI requirements that aren't negotiable—security, access, scalability, innovation, resilience, transparency, bias and more. Leverage talent.
9. Involvement/roles of key stakeholders. As projects are initiated, choose the correct stakeholders to oversee, manage and participate during the suitable phases. Allocate resources with an equal mix of experienced, proven and new stakeholders to ensure mentorship and growth. Your teams should emerge stronger, smarter and faster at the end of each initiative. Continuously improve.
10. Know your process and data readiness. Many projects have fallen under the scrutiny of process and data integrity. If your process transformation can't be envisioned upfront or the quality of data is not confirmed, AI isn't going to fix that. "Garbage in, garbage out" is still a thing. Prior proper planning (still) prevents poor performance.
11. Transform continuously. When processes change, people's roles and jobs change. Get ahead of this by offering a new career path that enhances your people's skill sets. Get them excited about change.
12. Create, leverage and keep champions and evangelists. Your people will grow and make amazing contributions, and that will make them attractive to your competitors. Ensure they know how they're valued, and reward them for their achievements. Don't assume you know what they want in their lives and careers. Ask and provide what you can to retain them, as they are your future. Keep them challenged and happy.
Enterprises that master these best practices and apply them to AI strategy and governance will be the winners. The ones that misread the signs and jump in too early or too late will struggle. By sharing our methods, learnings and best practices, we can help each other redefine what human intelligence is in the world of AI while using this unprecedented opportunity to make our enterprises stronger, better and more valuable to everyone on the globe. Embrace AI for the good of all.

title: How AI Is Powering The Indie Grocery Revolution
text:
When retail technology tools entered the grocery scene and quickly gained momentum, it was the big chains and e-commerce giants who were able to explore, adapt and get on board. This left regional and independent players in the dust as their larger counterparts grabbed the lion’s share of customer and revenue growth, with solutions like retail media networks and mobile apps enabled.
Fast-forward to today and independent grocers are getting their own tools to battle retail giants like Walmart and Amazon, thanks in large part to big data and the quickly evolving capabilities of AI and Machine Learning (ML) technologies.
Despite the rise of e-commerce, the data around customer behavior is clear: there is a continued preference for in-store shopping. According to a recent Prosper Insights & Analytics survey, 78.3% of customers have shopped in a physical store in the past 30 days.
32.6% of respondents are choosing to shop closer to home due to increased prices. For independent grocers who may be the go-to store for their communities, this is not just a trend, but a golden opportunity to enhance their digital technology and connect with shoppers in their own backyard.
The first crucial step is to establish the infrastructure needed to capture first-party data through a mobile app or website. Then, AI and ML will interpret that data, providing insights to enable personalized and efficient shopping experiences. By leveraging their strong community ties and utilizing their deep-data advantage, independent grocers can now develop content that is more relevant to the customer and thereby improve engagement.
Alasdair James, Chief Commercial Officer at Swiftly—a leader in retail technology solutions—highlights the unique position of independent grocers. “They're not just retailers; they’re at the heart of their communities, generating significant amounts of purchase data daily. Unlike the big chains, many of these local stores haven’t fully tapped into the potential of this data. Technological advancements in AI and ML are enabling independents to develop insights from their data, allowing them to provide more engaging and relevant content to their customers. This helps them compete with larger competitors and retail media networks for their customers' attention.”
In a recent Forrester-commissioned study titled AI Will Transform Retail, 41% of retailers shared that the direct impact that AI and ML have on customer experience is a top driver for investing in this technology. It allows them to connect with shoppers at various touchpoints, becoming especially impactful when integrated into loyalty programs that deliver personalized and relevant offers and ads that significantly enhance the shopping journey.
James elaborated, sharing that many grocers are leaning into solutions like “Just for You” recommendations, which not only identify products that have been purchased in the past but then deliver offers within the timeframe that they are regularly repurchased or are on sale. These programs are growing to be particularly important to shoppers as inflation continues to influence their purchasing decisions and habits.
Swiftly recently conducted their True Cost of a Grocery Shop survey and found that 82% of respondents use coupons, 64% participate in loyalty programs and 34% leverage retail apps. “These numbers show that a mobile-first strategy that focuses on data-informed, personalized experiences is a surefire way to drive customer engagement,” shared James. “The rise of digital circulars that deliver past-purchase-informed coupons and promotions are also proving to be extremely impactful and show an ongoing awareness of the importance of saving money for today’s shoppers.”
Also to consider is the impending deprecation of cookies and third-party data, which is set to impact the industry significantly. However, James sees this shift as an opportunity for independents to capitalize on their first-party data to create cost-saving and targeted experiences for their shoppers.
“By integrating AI and ML to really understand their first-party data, independent grocers can better understand their customers' preferences and behaviors,” James said. "When shoppers receive a personalized and therefore highly relevant digital coupon right when they're in the store, it feels like the store knows them and their needs. This immediate connection between customer preferences and real-time marketing is a game-changer for independent grocers that builds loyalty, and drives return visits that could otherwise be lost to competitors.”
Moreover, the use of AI and ML isn’t just about enhancing the shopping experience but also about the operational impact that retailers can take advantage of. Forrester’s study showed that 30% of respondents said the top driver for investing in AI was reducing operating costs, while 33% cited improved operational efficiency and effectiveness.
“AI can analyze vast amounts of data quickly and provide insights that would take humans much longer to uncover,” James explained. For example, AI can predict which products are likely to be in demand based on historical data, seasonal trends, and even local events. This predictive capability helps grocers manage their inventory more effectively, reducing waste and ensuring that popular items are always in stock.
Additionally, AI-powered customer service solutions can enhance operational efficiency for independents. "When you contact a retailer, you might be speaking to an AI-enabled system that directs your call based on the nature of your inquiry, reducing the need for human intervention and allowing staff to focus on in-store customers and operations," James said. This approach not only improves efficiency but also reduces costs for independent retailers.
AI and ML hold transformative potential for independent grocers. By embracing these technologies, independent grocers can not only stay relevant but lead the way in creating smarter, more personalized shopping experiences for their customers. Most retailers understand this, but the challenge historically has been one of cost. Operating in a low-margin environment, making the necessary investment to unlock such opportunities has previously been a significant financial risk. However, as these technologies continue to evolve and their costs decrease, the potential for innovation and growth within the independent grocery sector is now well and truly here.

title: The Tech Entrepreneurs Of Autism
text:
In the early 2010s, a wave of tech start-ups arose with the goal of employing adults with autism, building on the claimed skills of these adults in software testing and quality control. Most of these tech start-ups failed to survive: casualties of the offshoring and competitive price pressures of the software testing and quality control jobs they focused on, as well as an overhyping of the tech skills of most adults with autism. But a few of these start-ups have survived and even grown, and they point to possibilities in this niche market of employment going forward.
The wave of autism-focused tech start-ups was generated in good part by a glowing New York Times
Three start-ups from that period were able to navigate this competition, and continue to do so: AutonomyWorks, Ultranauts, and VenturesATL. Their success is due to the unusual skills and missions of the individual entrepreneurs who founded and continue to lead them, the teams they have built, and their ability to pivot and adapt to changing markets. Though the business lines of these companies differ, a common pivot has been to higher-level data and AI-related services.
This past month I went back to these three companies to get an update from their founders on their current employees, product lines and marketing, and how they see their company’s future, including the impacts of AI on staffing.
As summarized below, chief among their themes:
· They know they need to continue to adapt, given the current tech headwinds: These headwinds include the ongoing automation of basic data management functions, budget reductions for tech services among private sector companies, and the role of AI in eliminating entry level tech positions.
· Autism employment can be a marketing advantage in some cases, but it is not sustainable if the company does not perform: This advantage rapidly fades if the quality performance is not present.
· Increasingly they are facing tradeoffs between their employment goal of maximizing and diversifying job creation and their need adapt to automation and AI: The dual forces of automation and AI are increasing the roles for more experienced and skilled engineers, and reducing the number of employees needed in less skilled positions.
· Despite the competitive challenges, they have no plans to leave their roles, and hope to mentor a next generation of autism-focused businesses.
AutonomyWorks
1. Background: Launched in 2012 by David Friedman, and headquartered in Downers Grove, Illinois outside of Chicago. Prior to founding AutonomyWorks, Friedman served as president of marketing for Sears Holdings, and before that as an executive at Razorfish, the global marketing and technology company.
2. Current employees: As of May 2024, 75 employees, around 60 of them with autism or related conditions—up from the 12 employees a decade ago, in 2014. Employees are recruited mainly from the autism and neurodiversity organizations in the Chicago area.
3. Business lines: Three main business lines:
Data management – Audit and validate websites, product data, and production systems. Ensure compliance with standards, brand guidelines, and customer requirements.
Digital marketing operations – Implement and maintain digital marketing campaigns. Report and optimize performance.
AI/Automation – Build and manage data sets and processes necessary for the creation and management of artificial intelligence and automation solutions. A partnership with UiPath
4. Some of the Customers: MIQ (digital marketing), Grainger (data management), NEC Leasing (transaction processing), Dentsu (AI/automation).
5. Looking into the future: “I believe that autism-focused businesses have a future. People with autism really are talented. We see it every day in the work done by our team and in the feedback from our clients,” Friedman explains.
“I think that there are a few different options worth exploring in tech and beyond: (i) the place-based model (most of these businesses will be consumer oriented, but there are business-to-business models as well), (ii) supplier diversity, linking to the diversity initiatives in major companies, and (iii) focus/specialization: people with autism are most successful when they can build knowledge and expertise. By focusing narrower business or solution niches, autism focused businesses can build expertise and clearer differentiation.”
Ultranauts
1. Background: Founded in 2013, by Rajesh Anandan and Art Shectman, two MIT-trained engineers. Originally named ULTRA Testing and later changed to Ultranauts. Initially focused on software testing services, quickly evolved to quality engineering and test automation, then expanded to data governance, and recently launched a suite of AI products to improve team and individual workforce performance. Anandan has continued to the present as CEO.
2. Employees: Employees in 30 states, 75% of whom are neurodivergent. Job applicants sourced from a network of neurodiversity focused websites, blogs, influencers, and social media groups. Goal of ongoing upskilling of employees, as business evolves.
3. Business lines: 1. Software quality services launched in 2013 (software test automation, software quality diagnostic, quality engineering consulting), 2. Data governance services launched in 2019 (data quality management systems, data lineage solutions management), 3. HR technologies launched in 2023 (Team-X, Coach-X).
4. Some of the Customers: BNY Mellon, Comcast
5. Looking into the future: “Ultranauts plans to continue to evolve our core business of software quality and data governance services to keep pace with changing market needs. This includes the development of a new suite of services to help mid- market enterprises better leverage their data assets (with services like the CDO Accelerator, AI Pathfinder, and Data Governance in a Box) and a new defense-ready structure to provide quality engineering and test automation services to government customers and prime contractors. Ultranauts also plans to continue to develop and scale up our HR technology solutions including Team-X and Coach-X, which provide a path for the company to have a positive impact beyond its own organization and shape a more inclusive future of work for everyone.”
VenturesATL
1. Background: Founded in 2018 by the husband-wife team of Chet Hurwitz and Sara Barron, parents of a son with autism. Hurwitz, an attorney, had been a partner at PwC (formerly Price WaterhouseCoopers) and executive at IBM
